summaries.gardner: Abbott is a well-known, diversified healthcare leader with one fast-growing franchise (FreeStyle Libre), but it is a 138-year-old conglomerate, not the top dog of an emerging industry, and the stock has fallen about 19% over the past year. It fits Rule Breaker investing only loosely.
summaries.buffett: Abbott has durable consumer and medical brands, has paid dividends since 1924 and earns steady cash flow ($7,395M of free cash flow in 2025), which suits Buffett's preference for understandable, lasting businesses. Against that, returns on capital are modest (ROIC about 7.5%), debt jumped to $32.6B after the $23B Exact Sciences deal, and adjusted EPS has not grown since 2022.
summaries.munger: The business is easy to follow and diversified, with few ways to fail outright, but its moats are uneven: strong in CGM scale and installed lab systems, weaker in formula and generics. Munger would also weigh the recall history (Sturgis formula plant in 2022, Libre 3 sensors in 2026) as a quality-control risk.
summaries.lynch: Abbott is a classic stalwart: a big, steady company growing organically at about 6.5-7.5% a year with a 54-year record of dividend raises. At about 18 times forward earnings, against high-single-digit EPS growth, it is fairly priced for a stalwart rather than a Lynch bargain.
summaries.fisher: Abbott keeps developing new products (Libre 3 Plus, Lingo, Volt PFA, AVEIR, TriClip) and has a strong global sales force in 160+ countries, which matches several of Fisher's points. Its R&D spend is modest at 6.6% of 2025 sales, and margins have not clearly expanded over five years.
summaries.graham: Abbott passes Graham's size, dividend-record, ten-year-earnings and EPS-growth tests, but fails on price: about 21 times three-year average GAAP earnings and a P/E times P/B of about 120, far above 22.5. It would not qualify for a defensive Graham investor.
summaries.thiel: Abbott is not a zero-to-one company; most of its businesses sell into competitive markets with several large rivals. FreeStyle Libre, built on low-cost, high-volume sensor manufacturing, is the closest thing to a proprietary edge, but it is not ten times better than Dexcom.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price with operating discipline. Abbott offers steady mid-to-high-single-digit organic growth at about 18 times forward earnings, but it is not riding a major platform shift such as AI, and the Exact Sciences deal added leverage.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and strong price momentum, and Abbott has neither: the stock is down about 19% over 52 weeks and 2026 adjusted EPS guidance ($5.45-$5.60) implies only mid-to-high single-digit growth. Possible catalysts are Exact Sciences synergies and recovery from the Libre recall.
summaries.smith: Abbott has some Fundsmith traits: a resilient healthcare franchise, consumer brands and steady cash generation. Its returns on capital (about 7.5% ROIC) and 52.6% gross margin after amortization fall short of Smith's bar for high-return compounders, and the large acquisition goes against his preference for organic growth.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Abbott scores poorly: operating income of $8,053M against an enterprise value of about $210B is an earnings yield near 3.8%, and return on capital is modest because of large goodwill. It would not rank high on Greenblatt's screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, talented owner-minded management and the ability to reinvest at high rates. Abbott is a good business with competent management, but reinvestment returns have been modest and growth now relies partly on large acquisitions such as Exact Sciences.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary trouble bought at a deep discount. Abbott has had real setbacks (Libre recall, guidance cut, stock down 38% from its high by May 2026), but at about 18 times forward earnings with net debt near $27B it is not a heads-I-win, tails-I-don't-lose-much bargain.
summaries.wood: Abbott is not a disruptive-innovation platform in ARK's sense, although continuous glucose biosensors and multi-cancer blood tests (Cancerguard) touch ARK themes such as multiomic diagnostics. Its scale and diversification limit the exponential upside ARK seeks.
summaries.ackman: Abbott fits Ackman's taste for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating businesses with high barriers to entry in parts of its portfolio. Its leverage after Exact Sciences and its uneven growth fall short of Ackman's ideal, and there is no obvious activist catalyst.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep liked scale-economics-shared models. Abbott's Libre strategy of driving down sensor cost to widen access is a partial example, but the company as a whole is not built around passing savings back to customers.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought huge, fast-growing markets with technology-driven founders. Abbott is a mature conglomerate led by career executives; only its CGM and cancer-screening businesses address the kind of large, painful problems he favoured.
summaries.nash: Abbott fails several of Nash's hard filters: debt exceeds cash after the Exact Sciences deal, the 2025 operating margin was 18.2% (below 20%), organic growth is under 10%, and revenue growth plus FCF margin is about 22. It is a high-quality defensive company, but not the kind of high-growth, cash-rich secular winner Nash's process targets.

momentum.evidence: ABT closed at $104.89 on October 16, 2026, down about 19% over 52 weeks, and in May 2026 it was down 31.1% year to date while the Dow was up 5.4%.

g4.evidence: Abbott is run by experienced career managers under Chairman and CEO Robert Ford and is about 81% owned by institutions, but it has no famous founder or celebrity backer.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly call the stock undervalued after its fall: the average price target is $120.72 against a $104.89 price, and the forward P/E is about 18.

simple.evidence: Abbott has four understandable segments (Medical Devices $21,387M, Diagnostics $8,937M, Nutrition $8,451M, Established Pharmaceuticals $5,536M in 2025) selling everyday health products.

b2.evidence: Abbott has stayed profitable every year and raised its dividend 54 years in a row, but revenue swung with COVID testing (down 8% in 2023) and adjusted EPS of $5.15 in 2025 was below 2022's $5.34.

integrity.evidence: Abbott reports transparently and keeps a long dividend record, but it holds a combined chair/CEO role and has faced product-quality failures (the 2022 Sturgis formula shutdown and the 2026 Class I Libre 3 recall).

b6.evidence: Abbott mostly grows organically, but in 2026 it closed the $21B-equity / $23B-EV Exact Sciences acquisition, its biggest deal since St. Jude Medical in 2017.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 7.5% and ROE about 10.6% (StockAnalysis, October 2026), held down by large goodwill from St. Jude, Alere and now Exact Sciences.

fcf.evidence: In 2025 operating cash flow of $9,566M less capex of $2,171M gave $7,395M of free cash flow, more than GAAP net earnings of $6,524M.

b10.evidence: Adjusted EPS of $5.15 in 2025 was still below 2022's $5.34 despite years of retained earnings, and the shares at $104.89 (October 2026) are well below the $139.06 high of June 2025, so retained capital has not recently added matching value.

safety.evidence: At about 34 times trailing GAAP earnings and 23 times free cash flow, a conservative valuation does not show a wide margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of 18.1 is below many large medtech peers and Abbott's own history, but the PEG of 1.96 shows the growth on offer is modest.

mu5.evidence: Abbott is spread across devices, diagnostics, nutrition and pharma in 160+ countries, so no single product failure (such as the Libre 3 recall) is likely to sink the company.

reinvest.evidence: Abbott can reinvest in CGM, electrophysiology and cancer diagnostics, but returns on its overall capital base are only about 7.5%.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with a simple story: 6.5-7.5% organic growth guided for 2026, steady dividends and add-on growth from Exact Sciences.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 18 is well above expected adjusted EPS growth of about 7-10% (consensus FY2026 $5.52, FY2027 $6.07).

runway.evidence: CGM adoption (Diabetes Care +17.5% in 2025), pulsed field ablation and a $60B US cancer screening and precision oncology market cited by Abbott give it a long runway.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares edged down from 1,751M in Q2 2025 to 1,743M in Q2 2026 through buybacks, but there is no evidence of notable insider buying (insiders own about 0.5%).

ly8.evidence: Abbott is a $180B+ S&P 500 company covered by about 28 analysts, not an overlooked niche.

fi2.evidence: As COVID testing faded (from $1.6B in 2023 to $297M in 2025), Abbott pushed Libre 3 Plus, Lingo, Volt PFA, AVEIR and TriClip and bought Exact Sciences.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $2,942M (6.6% of 2025 sales) has produced growth drivers such as Libre and leadless pacing, but it is modest relative to device peers, and Abbott buys much of its innovation.

fi4.evidence: Abbott runs one of healthcare's broadest commercial networks in more than 160 countries, selling to hospitals, pharmacies and consumers alike.

longterm.evidence: Abbott took a $0.20 per share 2026 EPS hit to buy Exact Sciences for long-term growth, but it still manages tightly to annual EPS guidance.

gr1.evidence: Abbott had $44,328M of 2025 revenue and a market cap of about $181.5B in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: GAAP net earnings were positive every year from 2016 to 2025, with a low of $477M in 2017 (tax-reform charges) and $6,524M in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Abbott has paid dividends every quarter since 1924 and in December 2025 raised its dividend for the 54th consecutive year, to $0.63 per quarter.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS from continuing operations rose from $1.72 in 2015 to $3.72 in 2025, and adjusted EPS from $2.15 to $5.15.

gr6.evidence: Average GAAP EPS for 2023-2025 was about $4.87 ($3.26, $7.64, $3.72), so $104.89 is about 21.5 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 33.9 times P/B of about 3.55 is roughly 120, far above Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: Abbott's products are competitive but not ten times better than rivals; Dexcom, Medtronic and Boston Scientific offer comparable technology.

timing.evidence: The timing suits OTC biosensors, pulsed field ablation and blood-based cancer screening, but Abbott is late to PFA behind Boston Scientific's Farapulse.

th3.evidence: Abbott started as a broad 19th-century pharmaceutical company, not by dominating a small niche; Libre is the closest example of expanding from a niche.

team.evidence: CEO Robert Ford is a capable 30-year insider who led the St. Jude integration, but the team is solid rather than world-class founder-led.

th5.evidence: Abbott's global distribution through hospitals, labs, pharmacies and retail in 160+ countries is a major asset.

durable.evidence: Core lab installed base, formula brands and cardiac implants should last, but CGM and cancer screening face fast-moving rivals and new technologies.

th7.evidence: Abbott's markets are well known and contested by large rivals; it has not found a secret opportunity others miss.

trend.evidence: Abbott benefits from ageing populations and the diabetes epidemic but is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: 2026 adjusted EPS guidance was cut in April to $5.38-$5.58 (from $5.55-$5.80) for Exact Sciences dilution and only partly restored to $5.45-$5.60 in July.

dr2.evidence: By 2027-2028, Exact Sciences dilution should fade and the Libre recall be behind it, with consensus seeing FY2027 adjusted EPS of $6.07, about 10% above 2026.

dr4.evidence: Healthcare demand is largely economy-proof, but $32.6B of debt makes interest rates matter (Q2 2026 interest expense was $351M vs $525M for the first half).

dr6.evidence: Upcoming drivers include Q3 2026 results on October 21, Volt PFA and TriClip uptake, Lingo and Libre growth, and Exact Sciences cross-selling synergies.

dr7.evidence: With organic growth under 10%, a recent recall and weak momentum, conviction is not high enough for a concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 56.4% before amortization and 52.6% after in 2025, decent but below pure medtech peers such as Edwards (78.0%).

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 4.3% (P/FCF 23.2), reasonable for a defensive healthcare company but not cheap.

gb2.evidence: 2025 operating income of $8,053M is only about 3.8% of an enterprise value near $210B.

pa2.evidence: The 2026 setbacks (Libre 3 recall, COVID-testing decline, infant formula weakness, deal dilution) look mostly fixable, but formula and diagnostics softness may be structural.

pa4.evidence: Diversified, cash-generating businesses, 54 years of dividend increases and positive equity of $51,762M make permanent loss of capital unlikely.

wo1.evidence: Through Exact Sciences, Abbott now offers molecular cancer diagnostics such as Cancerguard and Oncotype DX, touching multiomics, but it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage or blockchain.

wo2.evidence: Libre sensor costs have fallen with scale, enabling cheaper and OTC products like Lingo, but this applies to only one part of the business.

wo3.evidence: It combines biosensors, molecular diagnostics and connected devices, but not in the converging-platform sense ARK describes.

wo4.evidence: Consensus sees revenue rising from $44.3B in 2025 to about $68B in 2030, about 1.5 times, not many times larger.

ac3.evidence: Demand is largely insulated, but Abbott is exposed to currency swings, interest on $32.6B of debt, and commodity and ingredient costs in nutrition.

ns1.evidence: Libre's low price, made possible by scale, has widened access and pressured Dexcom, but Abbott does not follow this model across the company.

ns4.evidence: Cancer diagnostics, PFA and biowearables could strengthen Abbott by 2036-2046, but formula and generics may weaken, so it is not clearly stronger.

va2.evidence: Diabetes, heart disease and cancer detection are large, painful problems affecting hundreds of millions of people.

tn1.evidence: Abbott sells into ageing and chronic-disease trends but is an old diversified company retrofitting into CGM and cancer screening, not one built for an AI-type secular trend.

tn2.evidence: The market still treats Abbott as a slow conglomerate hit by formula and COVID-testing declines, while Medical Devices is now 48% of sales growing over 10%.

tn3.evidence: Abbott is a $180B US large cap, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew in 2024 and 2025 and the company is profitable (2025 net earnings $6,524M), but it fails the cash test: debt of $32,608M vs cash and investments of $5,603M at June 30, 2026, a gap due to the Exact Sciences acquisition.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive, but debt exceeded cash at every recent quarter end, e.g. $12,929M of debt vs $8,939M of cash and investments at December 31, 2025, and $32,608M vs $5,603M at June 30, 2026.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 5.7% in 2025 and 2026 organic guidance is 6.5-7.5%; reported 2026 growth of about 13% is driven by the Exact Sciences acquisition.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 5.7% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 16.7% ($7,395M / $44,328M) is about 22, well below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 5.7% while total operating costs (cost of products sold, amortization, R&D, SG&A) grew 3.3%, from $35,125M to $36,275M.

tn9.evidence: It trips at least two instant kills: debt ($32,608M) exceeds cash ($5,603M), and the 2025 GAAP operating margin was 18.2%, below 20%.

tn10.evidence: Abbott faces NEC infant-formula lawsuits and FDA scrutiny after the February 2026 Class I recall of Libre 3 / 3 Plus sensors linked to 7 deaths and 860 serious injuries.

tn11.evidence: Abbott provides medical devices, diagnostic tests, nutrition and medicines that help patients and clinicians manage diabetes, heart disease and cancer, charging per device, sensor, test and product; customers choose it for low-cost CGM and broad, reliable test menus.

tn13.evidence: Total about 65/100: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0 (under 10% organic), operating margin 5, short interest 10 (0.79%), institutional ownership 10 (81%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2023 ($40,109M vs $43,653M), free cash flow fell from $8,648M in 2021 to $5,059M in 2023, and debt exceeded cash.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage (about 10.8x), current ratio (1.38) and liabilities/equity (about 1.1x) pass, but assets excluding goodwill ($73,971M) are only about 1.3 times liabilities ($57,453M), not 2x.

tn18.evidence: Ford has grown sales and launched products since becoming CEO in March 2020, but he has led for about 6.5 years, is not a founder, and has no notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Abbott usually meets its EPS guidance, but Q4 2025 sales of $11.46B missed the roughly $11.8B consensus, and Q1 2026 adjusted EPS of $1.15 only matched estimates.

tn21.evidence: There is no accounting or auditor red flag or co-CEO, but the $23B Exact Sciences deal and higher amortization pushed down GAAP margins in 2026 (Q2 net earnings $928M vs $1,779M a year earlier).

tn22.evidence: Abbott has $44B of revenue, real profits and steady buybacks, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: A free-cash-flow yield of about 4.3% implies perpetual growth of roughly 5-6% at a 10% discount rate, close to the 6.5-7.5% organic growth Abbott is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year averages (revenue growth about 0.7%, FCF margin about 14.8%), 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and net debt of about $27B, value comes out near $27 per share, far below $104.89.
